title: Administrators, You've GOT to Help Us With This ONE Thing Next Year
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing outside his usual classroom-teacher lane, Stuart makes a direct appeal to school administrators: lock in a consistent, school-wide cell-phone policy — specifically phone "garages" used in every classroom — before the next school year starts. He backs the ask with research citations on attention contagion, cognitive capacity, PISA score declines, and mental-health outcomes tied to phone bans, arguing the evidence question is already settled even if implementation isn't. The real argument of the piece is about leadership execution, not persuasion: most schools already have phone policies on paper, but they fail because administrators treat enforcement as optional and teacher-by-teacher rather than as a consistently led, non-negotiable school-wide system. He lays out a rollout sequence for administrators — align over the summer, communicate rationale to families at back-to-school events, train staff, and sustain visible reinforcement all year — modeled on interviews with two principals who implemented it successfully. The piece explicitly reframes this as leadership work administrators owe teachers, not something teachers should have to solve building-by-building through individual willpower.
points: Identifies the actual failure point of most school phone policies as inconsistent, discretionary enforcement rather than lack of a written policy — a leadership and systems problem, not a rules problem.
Recommends a specific low-cost mechanism (classroom phone garages) over confiscation-at-the-door systems, citing a principal's assessment of it as "the biggest bang for the buck educational move."
Lays out a full-year leadership cadence — summer alignment, back-to-school communication, staff PD, and ongoing visible reinforcement — rather than treating the policy as a one-time announcement.

Explicitly frames consistent phone-policy enforcement as an administrator's leadership obligation to teachers, comparing it to "hand-washing for doctors" — non-negotiable, not left to individual discretion.
quotes: Administrators, if you don't have a locked-in, 95%-consistent cell phone policy that lives and breathes and happens each day in your school, this summer your teachers and your students need you to lead the charge on a policy for making this happen.

As principal Ben Berger put it in our interview, leading the charge at his school on a solid, consistent, clear, and non-optional cell phone sleeve policy has been "the biggest bang for the buck educational move I've implemented.
This isn't an optional thing or something you leave up to professional discretion — this is like hand-washing for doctors.

Rinse and repeat these moves all year long, and you will find that a problem that used to riddle your school evaporates like a cold morning dew. There'll still be problems, but they won't be pervasive.
This type of leadership is NOT the job of your teachers, dear administrators — it is a part of your job as leaders. We need you to help us do "what's best for kids.
Unlike the latest buzzy trial headlines taking up our newsfeeds, the verdict has been in for a while on this matter of cell phones and secondary students.
